name: Aisha Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and I’ll keep your answers confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Aisha Dubois, 27, and I lead a small carpentry crew on housing sites. At seven I check the drawings, set out the day’s cuts, and then spend most of my shift measuring, fixing and helping the apprentices when a wall is out of square. I like seeing a frame stand straight by lunch; I hate chasing missing timber and being asked to make up for a late delivery.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do money and technology fit into that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earn more than most of our crew because I can run a job, and I’ve saved about nine months of living costs. I share a rented flat with my partner Noor, who teaches, and we have no children. I use an AI app every day to compare drawings and draft materials lists, but I check every measurement myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that AI Plateau sounds like another tool that makes the ordering easier. The saw and the pencil marks still need a person who knows which end of the timber is bowed. I wouldn’t sell a young apprentice a story that a phone can build a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the bigger risk is our usual stop-start building work, not clever software. My pay is good and there are several contractors nearby, but a quiet winter can still put a crew on short hours. I also know the boss likes any tool that lets one supervisor cover more sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and keep checking the AI materials list against the drawings each morning. This month I’d add a regular transfer to our savings, because I want a full year of rent and bills covered. In the first year I’d keep asking the apprentices to mark out by hand before they trust a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about my own work, though I’m never relaxed about a late site payment. My hands and my eye still earn their keep here. The young ones deserve time to learn the craft even when a program offers a shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a quiet winter mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor and I can pay our rent for nine months without my wages, which is a comfort I didn’t have at 20. If the site pauses, I’d take shifts with another builder before touching that fund. The fund buys us time, not a permanent holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which apprentice would feel even this small change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My apprentice Ravi is quick with an app but still checks a stair stringer twice with me. A tidy digital list doesn’t excuse a crooked stair. That lesson matters even if the software hardly changes.

say: I’d say **AI Plateau** helps with ordering, while people still build the frame.
I’d tell apprentices to **check measurements** by hand before trusting an app.
think: I’m more worried about a **quiet winter** than modest AI gains.
I suspect my boss may use software to stretch **supervisors** across more sites.
do: Keep leading the **carpentry crew** and checking each materials list against drawings.
Transfer money monthly until our savings cover **one year** of bills.
feel: **Steady** about my trade, with some worry about site payments.
S0.quote: A tidy digital list doesn’t excuse a crooked stair.
fieldNote: Her **nine-month cushion** and nearby builders give her room to weather an ordinary slow winter.
She keeps checking **materials lists** against drawings because bowed timber still needs a person on site.
She protects **apprentice practice** even when a phone offers a quicker answer.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew and checking AI materials lists against site drawings
Transfer part of each wage payment until savings cover one year of rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will clean up some paperwork and make us faster at ordering, if the builder shares the gain. I’d also say the crew needs paid training rather than a higher target every Monday. A good frame still needs people on the platform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d worry about the office staff and estimators first, because buying and checking plans are exactly what the card says AI takes. On site I could see fewer junior supervisors being hired, even while we still need carpenters. My own pay looks safe for now, but I don’t want my promotion to depend on someone else losing a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our union representative Lila to bring a training proposal to the next site meeting. Starting now, I’d learn the new estimating tools well enough to catch a bad order, and in the first year I’d run one paid session a month for my crew. I’d keep the savings transfer going as long as our rent stays where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy, mostly for people whose job is a screen and a phone. The site part of my work changes more slowly, so I can still picture a wage coming in. I’d be cross if faster ordering just turned into thinner staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets hurt first if ordering and checking change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our estimator Marta calls me when a drawing doesn’t match the actual slab. If her checking disappears, I want someone named as responsible for fixing the mistake before the frame goes up. The builder can’t call a computer accountable when a wall is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for at the site meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lila is the union representative for our site, not someone who can force the builder’s hand overnight. I’d ask for two paid hours each month and a written rule that a worker checks AI orders. If the boss refuses, I’d raise it with the crew rather than quietly train everyone on my own time.

say: I’d welcome **faster ordering** if the crew shares the gain.
I’d push for **paid training** before targets rise.
think: I fear **estimators** and junior supervisors could lose openings first.
I expect my own **site wage** to hold while carpentry stays hands-on.
do: Ask **Lila** to propose paid tool training at the site meeting.
Learn the **estimating tools** and teach one paid crew session each month.
feel: **Uneasy** for office staff, while still expecting my own wages to continue.
S1.quote: The builder can’t call a computer accountable when a wall is wrong.
fieldNote: She expects **estimators** to feel AI before carpenters, and worries that junior supervisor posts may thin out.
She wants **paid training** and a named worker responsible for errors in automated orders.
Her own wage looks safe for now, yet she resists faster ordering becoming a **staffing cut**.

steps.text: Ask union representative Lila to seek two paid AI training hours each month
Learn the new estimating tool and check its timber orders against drawings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that AGI by 2028 will hit drawings and buying before it can lift a sheet of plasterboard. I’d insist that a human signs off structural details and that nobody gets sent home on the strength of a screen alone. I can’t promise the site will stay the same once robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short, and I think my lead role could lose the planning and checking work that earns the extra pay. I’d still be useful with tools until capable robots show up around 2031, but that is a small window to build another specialty. Noor’s teaching might change too, and I don’t know how quickly schools would cut staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d ask the builder for a written skills plan and ask Lila to bring it to the union meeting. I’d enrol in an evening course on building inspections this winter, because a site still needs someone to spot defects and sign a record. In the first year after AGI arrives, I’d apply for inspection trainee posts while keeping my carpentry job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, and I wouldn’t hide that from Noor. We have savings and many builders nearby, so I can make a move without missing rent, but both our careers could be shaken. Three years after the software arrives is not very long in a working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor that week about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Noor that I want to pay the course fee from wages, not drain our emergency fund. We’d pause the idea of buying a flat until we know what both of us can earn after 2028. I’d also ask Noor what a change in school hours would do to our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still feel safe because the robots come later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead rate includes the days I catch an error before anyone cuts timber. If AGI does those checks cheaply, I might still have a job but lose that rate. A wage cut can reach our kitchen before a robot reaches our site.

say: I’d demand **human sign-off** on structural details when AGI handles plans.
I’d warn the crew that **2031 robots** could change physical work later.
think: I could lose my **lead rate** when AGI takes planning and checks.
I’m unsure whether **Noor’s teaching** income would remain steady.
do: Enrol in a **building inspection** course this winter.
Apply for **inspection trainee** posts during AGI’s first year.
Pause our **flat purchase** until both incomes are clearer.
feel: **Anxious** about two incomes, with savings enough to make a planned move.
S2.quote: A wage cut can reach our kitchen before a robot reaches our site.
fieldNote: The **2028 shock** could remove the planning and checking that earn her lead rate before robots reach the site.
Her **nine-month cushion** makes an inspection course and job applications possible without missing rent.
She and Noor would pause a **flat purchase** until they know both incomes after AGI.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening building inspection course this winter
Apply for building inspection trainee posts during the first year after AGI arrives
Pause the planned flat purchase until Aisha and Noor know their new earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our crew that AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to prepare for the change in drawings, orders and checks. I’d want the builder to publish a training timetable now, with wages protected while people learn. Robots come around 2034 in this picture, so the physical work has a little longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to qualify in inspections, but I’m not sure inspections will remain the same once AI can judge plans. I think the harder skill may be checking what has actually been built and explaining a fault to a client. I’d rather work alongside the new systems than wait for a letter saying my lead role has shrunk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start the inspection certificate next year and arrange one day a month shadowing the site inspector, if she agrees. Before 2031 I’d build a record of defects I found and fixed, without putting anyone’s private details into an app. In AGI’s first year I’d seek a quality-control post and keep site work until an offer is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert, not frightened. Noor and I could plan the course around our shifts and keep the savings intact. I would still worry about the apprentices if entry jobs become scarce before they get their hours on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for Ravi during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi would be 24 in 2031 and should have a proper trade by then if we give him the hours. I’d make sure Ravi gets time setting out stairs and frames, not just cleaning up after a machine. An apprentice cannot learn a crooked wall from a perfect simulation alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the builder will not fund the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the builder to pay for one course place per crew each year and to publish who gets those places. If the answer is no, I’d use part of my own training budget and apply to other builders that have inspection teams. I can afford a choice, but Ravi may not.

say: I’d ask for a **paid training timetable** before AGI changes site planning.
I’d remind the crew that **physical robots** arrive around 2034 in this picture.
think: I can qualify in **inspections**, though AI may also change that work.
I worry **apprentice hours** could disappear before younger workers master the trade.
do: Start an **inspection certificate** next year and shadow the site inspector monthly.
Keep a **defect record** to support a quality-control application after 2031.
feel: **Alert** and able to plan, with concern for apprentices.
S3.quote: An apprentice cannot learn a crooked wall from a perfect simulation alone.
fieldNote: The extra years let her earn an **inspection certificate** while keeping wages and collecting examples of defects fixed.
She questions whether plan inspection itself survives AGI and focuses on checking **built work**.

steps.text: Start an inspection certificate next year and shadow the site inspector one day monthly
Apply for a quality-control post in the first year after 2031 AGI arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that AGI by 2036 gives us time to shape how the site uses it. I’d want a real apprenticeship plan, not a promise that everyone can become a robot operator. The robots would arrive around 2039, so I’d still expect many years of hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036 I could have a full inspection qualification and still be young enough to switch again. I might also enjoy leading a crew that checks the work machines leave behind, though I don’t know whether that will be a proper job. Noor and I can decide about a home on our own timetable if our wages stay stable in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d build my inspection skills gradually and ask the builder to let me split one day a week between quality checks and carpentry by 2029. I’d keep the emergency fund and start a separate house deposit with Noor next year. In the first year after 2036 I’d take whichever paid site role uses both my hands and my inspection qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm because ten years lets me change course more than once. Building work has ordinary ups and downs, but my savings and nearby builders give me room. I’d be angry if the industry wasted that time and left new entrants with no way in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How old would you be when each change arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when AGI arrives, and 40 when the capable robots arrive around 2039. Those dates make it worth building a second skill while I’m still on site, rather than running away from the trade. I want to be able to point at something I helped build, even if my title changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make a home purchase during that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor and I would still talk about a flat, but we wouldn’t count an imagined future salary as a deposit. I’d put the extra lead-rate money into a separate account each month and review it with Noor every six months. If the builder cuts training, I can take that record of site work to another local firm.

say: I’d press for a **real apprenticeship plan** during the ten years before AGI.
I’d expect **hands-on work** to continue until capable robots arrive around 2039.
think: At **37**, I could hold an inspection qualification and still change course.
I can imagine a **mixed site role**, though its future pay is unknown.
do: Arrange a **quality-check day** each week by 2029 while keeping carpentry shifts.
Open a separate **house-deposit account** with Noor next year.
feel: **Calm** about my options, frustrated by any wasted training time.
S4.quote: I want to be able to point at something I helped build, even if my title changes.
fieldNote: A decade lets her blend **carpentry** with site quality checks before the physical robots arrive.
She keeps the **emergency fund** separate from a house deposit built with Noor.
She still wants a genuine **apprenticeship path** for entrants while she changes her own role.

steps.text: Split one day a week into building quality checks by 2029 to develop inspection skills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the planning side of my lead job could lose value before I finish a second qualification. Paid inspection training and a clear rule about who checks AI plans would help, and so would honest notice before any pay change. Our savings give me a runway, but they cannot replace a career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the first training place when a builder only pays for one. I can buy a course if I have to, but Ravi and other apprentices may not have that choice. A fair plan needs their names on it too.

headlineQuote: Our savings give me a runway, but they cannot replace a career.
portrait: Aisha, **27**, leads a carpentry crew and earns a higher wage for site planning and careful checks.
She and Noor rent together, have no children, and hold **nine months** of living costs.
She uses **AI daily**, yet insists that workers check drawings and built work.
She pursues **inspection skills** faster when AGI arrives sooner and presses for apprentices’ paid training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erode her lead rate before she completes an inspection qualification.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid inspection training**, human checks of AI plans, and clear notice before any pay change would help.
